Stuff from the States 

 

California

  • Pre-Rulemaking on Friction in Exercising CCPA Consumer Rights: Last fall, CalPrivacy previewed its rulemaking priorities for 2026. The agency has now started initial pre-rulemaking on two of those topics: reducing friction in the exercise of privacy rights and opt-out preference signals. The questions presented are fairly high-level and exploratory. For example, the agency asks “What challenges do businesses face in processing opt-out preference signals, like Global Privacy Control?” and “What challenges do businesses experience when they provide consumers with the ability to exercise their privacy rights, and how can the regulations address them?” The agency is accepting comments until 5:00 pm PT on April 6. 
  • Ninth Circuit Vacates in Part and Affirms in Part CAADCA Injunction on Appeal: The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed in part and vacated in part the District Court’s preliminary injunction against the California Age-Appropriate Design Code Act (CAADCA) in a ruling issued on March 12. In vacating parts of the order, the court held that the plaintiff had not met its burden for a facial challenge to the law’s coverage definition as a content-based regulation on speech and had not developed the record sufficiently for its facial challenge to the age estimation requirements.  However, the court affirmed the injunction against the data use provisions and dark patterns restrictions on vagueness grounds. Notably, related to the coverage definition reversal, the court found that NetChoice had not met its burden of developing a record that could allow a court to consider “every conceivable application of the CAADCA’s coverage definition,” including the kinds of activities and actors the law regulates, to demonstrate that the unconstitutional applications substantially outweigh the applications that do not. The court came to a similar conclusion with respect to the age estimation requirement, finding that the record did not sufficiently demonstrate how the age estimation requirement regulated protected speech in a substantial majority of its applications.

 

Kentucky - KCDPA Amendment on Smart TVs Reported from Committee (HB 692): The committee on Small Business & Information Technology favorably reported HB 692 on March 11. This bill would amend the KCDPA to add “automatic content recognition data” (data captured by a smart television or smart monitor) as a category of sensitive data.

 

Maine - Comprehensive Privacy Bill Passed Senate, Sent for Concurrence (LD 1822): Maine is inching closer to being the latest state to enact a comprehensive privacy bill after the Senate engrossed LD 1822. This is a Maryland-style bill that includes substantive data minimization requirements and a prohibition on selling sensitive data. The bill requires a concurrence vote as the House and Senate floor amendments do not match. You can find FPF’s overview of that bill as well as an unofficial redline showing recent amendments in the FPF Portal here.

 

Nebraska - AADC Amendment Passed Committee (LB 1119): This bill passed out of committee and was placed on general file with an amendment on March 11. Notably, the proposed amendment would change the Act’s scope to provide a new exemption for GLBA regulated entities, and cover an online service that “generates a majority of its annual revenue from online services.”

 

South Dakota - Genetic Privacy Bill Passed Legislature (SB 49): South Dakota is poised to become the latest state to enact a direct-to-consumer genetic testing privacy law after the legislature passed SB 49 this week. This bill would regulate direct-to-consumer genetic testing, including by providing for consumer data rights, consent requirements, and data security obligations. It has not yet been sent to the governor to be signed or vetoed. 

 

Utah - Motor Vehicle Privacy Bill Passed Legislature (HB 357): The Utah legislature passed an amendment to the Utah Consumer Privacy Act last Friday. This bill has not yet been sent to Governor Cox to sign or veto. If enacted, the bill would amend the UCPA to (1) apply to any motor vehicle manufacturer who manufactures motor vehicles that are sold or leased in Utah and collects, transmits, or stores personal data through a vehicle data collection system, and (2) require motor vehicle manufacturers to implement certain in-vehicle privacy controls. You can find FPF’s two-page overview of this bill on the FPF Portal here.
